doc.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: LP side length, High Fly and the 6/8 tunes
summary: He explains LP timing, putting High Fly first on side two as a hedge, and Randy Weston's and Cannonball's 6/8 numbers.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Plus at that time, how long was a side of an LP?
Well you wouldn’t want to be much over twenty minutes.
Okay. So your time was in a sense a little more valuable too. To give up a minute twenty for someone talking.

Oh yeah. But nevertheless I just felt this was such a characteristic of the guy, and we did the same thing, because if you can remember back before the CD, there was side one and there was side two. And since one might be marked one, your second most important spot on an LP, and for audience attention but more particularly for disc jockey attention, was the first tune on the second side. See that no longer exists now when old LPs are translated into CDs, that’s just something in the middle. But we actually were hedging our bets just a little bit on that one. We thought, judging from audience reaction that “This Here” was going to be the monster breakout song that it turned out to be. But we weren’t a hundred percent sure, and it was another number that got tremendous reaction, this was the first recording as far as I know of Randy Weston’s “High Fly” which of course has become quite a classic in its own right, and so we put that as the first number on the B side, as a back-up. And that’s got a wonderful — it also starts with Cannon talking. And he talks about how Randy Weston, a lot of whose best numbers were in 6/8 and that Randy Weston has become to be known in jazz circles as the waltz king. And he says I don’t mean Wayne King. But so we had a talk introduction on each side. We were hedging our bets but going for broke with the talk concept.
It’s interesting that both of those tunes are 6/8 feels. Who would expect?

He got into 6/8 a lot. And what he said was of course one of the things, he said like the bad thing about having a hit is you’ve got to play it every God damn night probably every God damn set. But he said that one was always a lot of fun, “This Here” because audiences would feel impelled to rhythmically clap along with it, but for the most part they didn’t have the faintest idea that it was in 6/8. So they were in there clapping on two and four, you know. © Fillius Jazz Archive -21-
